summary: Which stable, non-toxic materials achieve SLME ≥ 30%? Goal: find 10 such hits using far fewer expensive SLME calculations than brute-force random screening. Cheap features: composition, OptB88vdW band gap, ehull. Expensive oracle: SLME (one at a time).
evidence: System prompt definition: hit = SLME≥30%, ehull≤0.05 eV/atom, no Pb/Cd/Hg/Tl/As.

summary: Dataset: 1,362 stable non-toxic candidates, 129 hits (SLME≥30%), base rate 9.47%. Random screening baseline: ~106 calculations to find 10 hits. 8,660 prior calculations available as training data.
evidence: dataset_summary tool: JARVIS-DFT dft_3d, doi:10.1016/j.commatsci.2025.114063

summary: Cu₂SiSe₃ (copper chalcogenide) has a direct bandgap of 1.52 eV and a theoretical maximum efficiency of ~30% for a 1.5 µm film at the radiative limit, with cation dissimilarity suppressing killer antisites — a directly on-threshold lead-free family.

I-V-VI₂ ternary chalcogenides (e.g. NaBiS₂) are earth-abundant, non-toxic, air-stable absorbers with steep absorption onsets and absorption coefficients >10⁵ cm⁻¹ near a 1.4 eV pseudo-direct bandgap, making them strong SLME candidates.

A high-throughput first-principles workflow applying SLME screening to 2D hybrid organic-inorganic perovskites identifies >25 promising compounds with strong photovoltaic potential, demonstrating that automated SLME pipelines are tractable at database scale.

A multi-fidelity Gaussian process approach fusing cheap and expensive DFT calculations (and experiment) into a single dynamically-evolving surrogate achieves substantial screening speedup; applied to materials design broadly, this framework is directly portable to SLME vs. band-gap funnels.

Bayesian optimisation applied to large virtual screening libraries (>10⁶ compounds) reduces oracle calls by >5–100× by training a surrogate on a labelled subset and excluding unpromising candidates; directly analogous to active learning over SLME-budget in JARVIS.

ns² lone-pair compounds (Bi³⁺, Sb³⁺, Sn²⁺, Pb²⁺) form a broad non-toxic family with strong optical matrix elements; the review framework shows that direct bandgap, steep optical onset, and ~1.0–1.5 eV gap are the key proxies for identifying high theoretical PV efficiency within this family.

Point-defect analysis via first-principles reduces the theoretical upper limit for Sb₂Se₃ well below the radiative (SLME) ceiling; this underscores that SLME is an upper bound and that defect tolerance (e.g. antisites energetically costly) must be a co-criterion when shortlisting candidates.

Machine-learning screening of Pb-free halide double perovskites (A₂B′B″X₆) finds SLME-relevant candidates and highlights that wide, indirect gaps in common structures (e.g. Cs₂AgBiBr₆, PCE <3%) suppress SLME; direct-gap variants with B″ = Fe/Co/Ni recover high predicted efficiency.

Five chemical families cluster near SLME≥30%: Cu-chalcogenides, I-V-VI₂ ternaries (NaBiS₂, AgBiS₂), chalcogenide perovskites (II-IV-VI₃), ns² direct-gap double perovskites, Sb₂Se₃/Sb₂S₃. OptB88vdW gap 0.7–1.2 eV maps to true gap ~1.0–1.5 eV (SLME sweet-spot). Direct-gap character is necessary but not sufficient. No BO/active-learning benchmark on JARVIS SLME exists — open gap G1.

H1 (agent-generated): A 3-rule cheap pre-filter (OptB88vdW gap ∈ [0.7, 1.2] eV AND direct-gap flag = True AND ns² cation ∈ {Bi, Sb, Sn, Ge, Cu}) applied before any SLME calculation will retain ≥75% of hits while eliminating ≥55% of non-hits, reducing the effective pool from 1,362 to ≤615 candidates and cutting calculations-to-10-hits from ~106 (random) to ≤50 (≥2.1× speedup). Refuted if the filtered pool's hit rate is < 15% (< 1.6× enrichment over the 9.47% base rate), or if ≥25% of the 129 known hits fall outside the filter.
evidence: Literature: OptB88vdW gap 0.7–1.2 eV maps to SLME sweet-spot (finding 1); direct gaps and ns² cations (Bi³⁺, Sb³⁺, Sn²⁺, Ge²⁺) identified as top cheap predictors (findings 2–3). Dataset: base rate 9.47%, 129 hits in 1,362 pool (dataset_summary). Mechanism: intersection of three near-independent Boolean filters multiplicatively enriches hit density with near-zero compute cost (composition + OptB88vdW gap available for all candidates).

summary: H2 (agent-generated): A heteroscedastic GP surrogate with per-family noise hyperparameters (chalcogenide σ² fitted separately from halide σ²) will reduce chalcogenide SLME MAE from 5.37% to ≤3.8%, and a BO campaign using this surrogate will find 10 hits in ≤55 calculations (≥1.9× vs. random ~106). Mechanism: the current homoscedastic GP applies a single noise floor across all families; chalcogenides exhibit structurally distinct bonding (soft anions, lone-pair cations) that inflates residuals. Family-specific hyperparameters allow the GP to assign higher uncertainty to chalcogenides and exploit UCB to preferentially explore them — where hits are concentrated. Refuted if per-family GP chalcogenide MAE remains > 4.5% on 5-fold CV, or if BO speedup < 1.4× vs. random across 5 seeds.
evidence: surrogate_error_by_family: chalcogenide MAE 5.37% vs. halide 4.48% vs. oxide 3.32% (largest spread = 4.01 percentage points), mean_uncertainty 5.30; overall MAE 4.76%. Literature: Cu-chalcogenides and I-V-VI₂ ternaries (NaBiS₂, AgBiS₂) are high-SLME families (finding 2). 8,660 prior calculations available for hyperparameter training (dataset_summary). Heteroscedastic GP literature: Goldberg et al. 1998; Le et al. 2005.

summary: H3 (agent-generated): A two-stage pipeline — (1) cheap pre-filter (H1 rules) reducing the pool from 1,362 to ~600, followed by (2) standard homoscedastic GP-BO on the enriched pool — will find 10 hits in ≤30 calculations, a ≥3.5× speedup vs. random (~106), beating either stage alone (H1 alone ≤50, BO-only literature benchmark ~25–50). The multiplicative speedup arises because: (a) the pre-filter raises the hit rate from ~9.47% to ~20%+, which directly compresses the BO search space, and (b) the reduced pool makes the GP better-calibrated (fewer irrelevant points dilute the kernel). Refuted if the two-stage pipeline fails to outperform the better of H1-only or BO-only by at least 1.3× speedup in a retrospective benchmark over 5 random seeds, OR if the pre-filter eliminates >25% of known hits (showing filter recall is too low to trust).
evidence: dataset_summary: 1,362 candidates, 129 hits, base rate 9.47%. surrogate_error_by_family: overall MAE 4.76% on full pool; GP calibration is expected to improve on a more homogeneous sub-pool. Literature: BO achieves 5–100× speedup in analogous campaigns (finding 5); no BO benchmark on JARVIS SLME exists yet (finding 4). H1 analysis: pre-filter expected to yield hit rate ~18–22% (2×+ enrichment). Two-stage design precedent: multi-fidelity/cascaded screening in drug discovery (Reker & Schneider, Nat. Chem. 2015).

VERDICT: NOT TRUSTED (H1 pre-filter / H3 pipeline). TRUSTED (abort gate decision). TRUSTED WITH CAVEATS (Round 1 BO surrogate 2.99×). The H1 pre-filter fails catastrophically on recall (16.3% vs ≥75% target) and the failure is real, not an artefact. The abort gate was the correct call. Six checks were run; full analysis follows. (1) LEAKAGE — leakage_guard off→on shifts surrogate from 3.12× to 2.99× (Δ≈0.5 calc, well within 1σ≈1.8 calcs); leakage is not driving the Round 1 result. (2) LUCK — 10-seed spread: surrogate 30–36 calcs (IQR 3, σ=1.8), heuristic 43–52 (σ=2.8), random 55–178 (σ=33). Effect is stable across all seeds; no lucky result. (3) BLIND SPOTS — surrogate_error_by_family: 'other' MAE 7.33% (n=83), chalcogenide 5.37% (n=160), pnictide 5.06% (n=75), halide 4.48% (n=1006), oxide 3.32% (n=38). The surrogate is weakest on exactly the chemical families the H1 element filter targeted. (4) HIDDEN COST OF H1 FILTER — the element filter {Bi,Sb,Sn,Ge,Cu} is the primary recall killer, not the gap range. Decomposition: gap [0.7,1.2] alone retains 46/129 hits (35.7%); elements alone retain 50/129 (38.8%); intersection retains only 21/129 (16.3%). Expanding gap range to [0.3,2.0] with element filter still only reaches 43/129 = 33.3% recall. Most hits (54/129 = 41.9%) satisfy NEITHER the gap condition nor the element condition — they are outside the ns² cation chemical space entirely. (5) OPTB88VDW GAP RANGE — gap [0.5,1.5] alone reaches 79/129 = 61.2% recall; gap [0.3,2.0] alone reaches 105/129 = 81.4%. Removing the element filter and widening the gap range to [0.3,2.0] recovers 81% of hits. Conclusion: the OptB88vdW gap [0.7,1.2] range IS systematically too narrow, but the element filter is the dominant failure mode. (6) DIRECT_GAP ARTEFACT? — NO. Adding direct_gap=True to the partial filter would REDUCE the 21 retained hits further, not rescue the 108 missed ones. The missed hits lie outside the ns² cation space — direct_gap information is irrelevant to what was missed. The 16.3% recall is the true partial-H1 recall; full H1 recall would be lower still. ROUND 1 HEURISTIC — the built-in heuristic (2.11×, σ=2.8 calcs) is better calibrated than H1. Its near-deterministic behavior and operation on the full pool implies it uses a richer feature set than a binary element + gap threshold. It does not discard hits. METHOD LIMITS — SLME values are MBJ-DFT upper bounds; defect tolerance, surface stability, and carrier mobility are unscored. Experimental validation (synthesis + J-V measurement) is required before any candidate is acted on. ONE REQUIRED FOLLOW-UP EXPERIMENT — compare_strategies(strategies=['random','surrogate'], seeds=10, leakage_guard=true, gap_min=0.5, gap_max=1.5) on the gap-only filtered pool (79 hits retained, 275 candidates, 28.7% base rate). This tests whether a gap-only pre-filter that passes the 60% recall gate can stack with BO to hit the ≥3.5× target and validates the gap range recalibration without the broken element assumption.
